analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to test algorithms used in hiring, lending, housing, and benefits for bias before using them.
analysis.headline: Introduced on December 2, 2025 with 29 Democratic cosponsors, the bill sits with two House committees and has received no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make companies check their algorithms for discrimination before using them in decisions that shape people's lives, like hiring, lending, housing, insurance, and government benefits. Anyone whose algorithmic decision harms them could appeal to a human, sue for damages, and see the audit results posted publicly. Enforcement would go through the Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits: People subject to algorithmic decisions about jobs, credit, housing, insurance, education, health care, criminal justice, elections, and government benefits. The bill targets discrimination based on race, sex, disability, age, income, and other protected traits, and gives individuals the right to a human decision, an appeal, and a court case free of forced arbitration.

how_it_helps.text: Before an algorithm is used for a 'consequential action' (hiring, pay, education, housing, utilities, health care, credit, insurance, criminal justice, elections, benefits, and more), the company must run a preliminary harm check and, if harm is plausible, a full independent audit covering how the algorithm was built, trained, and tested, and its potential for disparate impact on protected groups.
After deployment, companies must run annual impact assessments, report findings to the FTC within 30 days, publish summaries on their websites, and keep records for at least 10 years.
Individuals gain a right to opt out of an algorithmic decision and have a human decide instead, plus a right to appeal to a human, both to be set by FTC rules and available at no cost.

The FTC, state attorneys general, and individuals can enforce the rules; individuals can recover treble damages or $15,000 per violation, and pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers cannot be used to block these claims.

The FTC must publish a public, searchable repository of algorithm audits, cannot be blocked by trade secrets beyond redaction, and may hire up to 500 additional staff; a new federal occupational series for algorithm auditing would be created.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that build or use covered algorithms: AI developers and the businesses deploying them in hiring, lending, insurance, tenant screening, benefits, and similar decisions would bear audit costs, reporting obligations, exposure to lawsuits with treble damages and $15,000-per-violation state penalties, and lose the ability to force these disputes into arbitration.
analysis.who_pays_short: AI developers and businesses using algorithms

drawbacks.text: Compliance is costly and repetitive: every covered algorithm requires a preliminary evaluation, possible full independent audit, annual impact assessments, disclosures in 10 languages, and 10-year record retention, a burden that falls hardest on small businesses using off-the-shelf tools.

Liability is broad: a private right of action with treble damages or $15,000 per violation, enforceable against both developers and deployers, invites litigation even where no one was actually harmed, and companies can redact trade secrets from the public audit reports, limiting how much the public can verify.

The bill's scope is defined by FTC rulemaking in large part, so the actual burden depends on how aggressively the commission writes the rules; an adversarial or lax FTC could make the protections far weaker or the compliance burden far heavier than the text suggests.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are substantial and aimed at a real, growing problem: automated decisions that few people can see or contest. The honest tradeoff is cost and litigation exposure, particularly for small businesses, and the possibility that audits become a paperwork exercise rather than real accountability. The bill's design leans toward strong enforcement, with public reporting and damage multipliers, which raises both its potential benefit and its compliance burden.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in December 2025 and sent to the Energy and Commerce and Oversight committees, where no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Yvette D. Clarke of New York introduced the bill on December 2, 2025, joined by 22 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The Speaker referred it to two committees, Energy and Commerce and Oversight and Government Reform, for consideration of the provisions within each committee's jurisdiction.
The bill has 29 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further action has been taken since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no outcome has been reached. If the bill stalls without action, AI developers and the businesses that deploy algorithms in consequential decisions are better off, avoiding audit requirements, reporting, and litigation exposure; consumers harmed by algorithmic decisions gain nothing until a law passes.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No outcome yet; algorithm users benefit if it stalls

sides.party_line_note: All 29 cosponsors, including the sponsor, are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits in committees controlled by the House Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill requires independent audits before deployment, annual impact reviews, public disclosures, and exposes developers to treble-damages lawsuits and a ban on forced arbitration for these claims. Their commercial interest in avoiding these costs runs against the consumer protections the bill creates.

industries.industry: Deployers of algorithms (employers, lenders, insurers, landlords, benefits administrators)
industries.note: Any business using an algorithm for hiring, credit, housing, insurance, or benefits must run harm evaluations, offer human alternatives and appeals, and share liability with developers. Cost falls on them; the benefit of contestable decisions accrues to the public.
The bill creates a mandated market for independent bias audits and a new federal occupational series for algorithm auditing, building a profession around the required assessments.

industries.industry: Federal Trade Commission and state enforcers
industries.note: The FTC gains explicit jurisdiction over algorithmic discrimination, including over common carriers, banks, and nonprofits usually outside its reach, and may hire up to 500 staff; state attorneys general gain $15,000-per-violation or 4%-of-revenue penalties.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is at the starting line: newly introduced, referred to two committees, no Republican cosponsors, and no scheduled action. A partisan bill with no committee activity at this stage typically dies quietly at the end of the Congress. It could advance only if a committee schedules a hearing or markup, which currently shows no sign of happening.
